design ceiling q10 / median / q90 below census gap a2 median gap a2 positive mean interval
uniform 0.557 / 0.746 / 0.847 37.5% -0.054 37.5% 0.606
uncertainty 0.233 / 0.403 / 0.507 100% 0.194 92.5% 0.867

The tilt’s bias is absolute rather than typical. Not one draw in forty reached the corpus figure, and the ninetieth percentile of the tilted ceiling, 0.507, sits below the tenth percentile of the uniform one, 0.557. The two distributions do not overlap. A researcher drawing that way is not unlucky sometimes, they are wrong every time.

And it flips the finding. The gap against annotator2 came back positive on 92.5 percent of tilted draws against 37.5 percent of uniform ones, where the census says -0.004. Nearly every tilted sheet says the model beats the human ceiling on a coder the corpus says it merely ties.

The uniform draw is not unbiased at twenty rows, and the two biases offset. Its ceiling median is 0.746 against a census 0.701, with only 37.5 percent of seeds below, so the coefficient runs about 0.045 high at this size. The gap median runs about 0.050 low, which is the same effect arriving through coder_alpha in the denominator of the comparison. That is small-sample behavior of alpha rather than anything the design does, and it is worth knowing before quoting a ceiling off twenty rows to three decimals.

The tilt widens the interval by 43 percent, 0.867 against 0.606. It is not a precision trade at all on this comparison.

The seed the article shows is the tilt at its most extreme. 0.212 sits below the tenth percentile of tilted draws, where the typical is 0.403. Step 5 says the direction is not seed-specific rather than leaving one draw to stand for the distribution.

Route A ships, and the bake’s own criterion decided it. The three-level runs behind the figures below left the bake in 5.33, after route A shipped. Six levels separated cleanly, at 0.17, 0.15, 0.13, 0.18, 0.18 and 0.19 of the hundred against the 0.167 apiece an even spread would give. That was the condition, and one level taking nearly everything was the failure mode.

The nominal ceiling came in at 0.480 against the paper’s 0.543, and the three-level one at 0.579 against 0.656. Both undershoot by a similar margin, which is what a hundred-sentence subsample of a larger corpus does rather than a defect in either reading.

The criterion’s other prediction also held. On three levels the nominal and ordinal ceilings are 0.579 and 0.617, a difference of 0.038, against 0.480 and 0.701 on six. The ordinal metric has almost nothing to demonstrate at three levels and earns its keep at six, which is where the coders’ own design put it.

6.3 Why the corpus interval uses Hartley-Rao

Retired with the corpus row. The interval it measured belonged to a weighted estimate the package no longer makes. See 5.30.

6.4 Costs

A bootstrap replicate costs about 0.70ms when the ratings go in as a character matrix and 1.95ms as a data frame, because kripp_parts() coerces internally. Everything on the resampling path builds matrices for this reason.

2000 replicates cost roughly 1.5 seconds per question on validate_sample() and about 7.4 seconds per question on the ceiling with three coders, since every replicate recomputes alpha once per pair and once overall. ci = "none" is the default so nobody pays unless they ask.

6.5 Moved out of the published docs

Figures and reasoning that left the help pages and the validation vignette when they were cut back to what a function does and what each number is. Kept here so the record survives. The pitch, loudness, diarization and per-image token figures the FAQ left out are already in section 9, and the coverage, tilt and width figures the validation vignette left out are in 6.2 and 6.3.

Case folding goes through stringi. From ?instrument. Folding runs through stringi rather than base toupper(), which is locale dependent for non-ASCII. Under LC_CTYPE = "C" base folding leaves an accented character untouched, so an accented label would stop matching its own uppercase form with no error raised anywhere.

bytes stands in for resolution. From ?prepare_image. bytes comes from file.size(), and it stands in for resolution well enough that a corpus of comparable images sorts the same either way. Width and height would need a format-aware reader and nothing yet asks for them.

Frames are written beside the recording, not to a temporary directory. From ?prepare_video. A temporary directory would break three things. coding_sample(copy_media = TRUE) could not copy the media beside a sheet, a saved corpus could not be reloaded in another session, and the cache would point at files that are gone.

select = "change" concentrates. From ?prepare_video. On one four-minute clip it left the first 76 seconds with a single frame because nothing in it moved. min_gap is what stops that.

Interval width and the census bins on parlasent. From interpreting-validation, since dropped. Forty draws of twenty coded rows on the parlasent corpus returned intervals averaging 0.81 wide on a scale running from -1 to 1. The parlasent census returns 0.3, 0.4, 0.4, 0.5, 0.3, 0.4, 0.9, 0.7, 0.9, 0.9 across ten bins of ten. A step rather than a gradient, with the break near a winning probability of 0.99999.

6.6 The label order on the six-level run

The bake over every document, order_sensitivity() on res_six with all 100 sentences, seed = 444 and the ordinal metric over 1 to 6.

order n agreement alpha
reversed, 6 5 4 3 2 1 100 0.75 0.936
shuffled, 6 3 5 1 4 2 100 0.77 0.903

Reversal changed 25 winners and the shuffle 23. An ordinal alpha that high beside a quarter of the winners changing means the changes ran mostly between nearby levels. On the same bake and the same 100 sentences, the model’s ordinal alpha with the coders was 0.733 and the coders’ with each other 0.701. The audit sets the model against itself rather than against a coder, so the comparison is a scale rather than a test. The order moves the model’s answers less than one coder’s answers differ from another’s. The first bake drew 50 sentences and changed 13 and 9 winners, at alphas of 0.936 and 0.955.

7. Working protocol

For a future session. Learned expensively, mostly by shipping the failure first.

7.1 Patches

git apply-ready files. State the base md5 before delivery and the result md5 after. Build in a scratch tree, apply to a clean copy of the base, and compare byte-for-byte against the scratch build before shipping. Never combine unrelated changes in one patch unless Gorsky agrees. Structural changes precede voice changes.

State tracking is yours. Apply every delivered patch to your own reference tree in the same turn he reports running it, and print the resulting digests. Audit by content, not by git apply --check --reverse, which gives false negatives whenever two patches share an insertion anchor or a file has been replaced wholesale.

Every patch states the base and result md5 of each file it touches. That table does what a document-wide digest table used to do, scoped to what the patch can break, and the base column is checked before the patch is built rather than after it fails.

devtools::check() before devtools::test(). check() catches broken Rd cross-references and test() does not.

7.2 The mechanical gates

Four checks, each of which exists because the failure it catches was shipped. Run all four before delivering anything that touches a message, a test, or a return shape.

A document() cascade against a clean source is the session, not the file. Fifteen warnings out of one devtools::document(). \value{} never closed, every later section read as an unexpected header, the file ended inside a brace, and the first warning named a section forty lines past anything that could be wrong.

Nothing was wrong. The same tree produced a clean document(), check() and test() from a fresh R console. What the old session was holding is not known and is not worth finding out.

Four clean gates against a file the generator calls broken is the finding. Brace balance per roxygen block, brace balance per tag, every \item{} in a \describe{} carrying its second argument, and even backtick counts per tag so an unterminated code span cannot swallow a brace into a \code{} where roxygen escapes it. All four came back clean while document() kept reporting. That combination means the generator is not reading what you are reading, and the next move is a restart, then readLines() on the generated .Rd, and only then the source.

Read in the wrong order it cost a patch shipped on a guess, and a paragraph in this document asserting a mechanism that was never demonstrated. The four gates above are worth keeping and each catches something test() does not. The mechanism that entry described does not exist.

The one-paragraph \item{} bodies that patch left behind stay, because they match the eleven items above them, not because they repaired anything.

The assertion gate. Every expect_error/warning/message pattern in tests/ checked against every fmt_*-wrapped message in R/, at the real 80-column wrap, using the package’s own fmt_lines() and fmt_err() sourced out of R/utils.R. Three buckets, broken by the wrap, unmatched by any message, and fine. Unmatched is not benign. It is the signature of an assertion left stale by a reworded message, which is how the same test broke twice.

Patterns are regexes, so \s+ at every space is the robust form. A single well-placed \s+ breaks the moment the message length changes and the wrap moves somewhere else.

Build every patch against the tree the last one produced. Patch 32 failed to apply because its design-doc hunk was written against a copy two patches stale. The intervening hunks had not overlapped, so git apply had accepted them and the two trees diverged silently while every digest check passed, since each was checked against its own base rather than against the live one.

The fix is 7.1’s rule taken literally. Apply every delivered patch to the reference tree in the same turn it is reported run, and copy the next patch’s base from that tree rather than from a scratch directory that may have forked.

A stub that only records is half a stub. The image probe passed base64 where ollama_generate() takes a path, so it encoded an already-encoded string and reported itself as having failed rather than as having been misused. A capturing stub that stored what it received and asserted nothing let that through. Where a mock stands in for something that reads the world, it should check what it was handed, file.exists() and a plausible size here, not only that an argument arrived.

A stub is a contract with the function it replaces. helper-offline.R mocks ollama_generate(), so adding an argument there and not to both stubs made every offline call fail with unused argument, every row come back ok = FALSE, and 70 tests fail on empty results with nothing naming the cause. check() reported it as 70 unrelated failures across four files.

And the stubs are not only in the helpers. Fixing helper-offline.R alone left seven more, one in helper-fixtures.R, four in test-backend.R and two in test-pipeline.R, written inline where a test wanted a particular reply. Nine sites for one function, and the second round of failures came entirely from the seven the first fix did not reach.

So the sweep is over all of tests/, not over the helper file.

grep -rn "function(prompt, backend" tests/

The general form matches the first two argument names of every function in tests/ against every function in R/ and reports any whose lists then differ, which finds a drifted stub whatever it is called and wherever it was written.

The same holds for objects the helpers fake. stub_backend() builds a fathom_backend by hand, so a field added to ollama_backend() has to be added there too or the stub exercises a fallback rather than the object under test.

Check every fathom::: name in tests/ against what R/ defines, after any rename. The assertion gate compares message patterns and says nothing about identifiers, so a renamed internal function leaves object not found for test() to find rather than for a gate to. Three call sites of fathom:::as_texts survived a rename this way and reached a check().

grep -ro "fathom:::[A-Za-z._][A-Za-z0-9._]*" tests/ | sort -u

Never re-copy a file mid-patch. Both of the breaks above came from one mistake. A rename was applied across nine files, then test-audit.R was re-copied from the reference tree to add tests to it, and the second copy carried none of the first pass’s edits. Build every change to a file in one pass, and if a second pass is needed, take it from the working copy rather than from the base.

A field name shared across two levels of a format is a silent-wrongness trap. prepare_audio() read the word token as word or, failing that, text. A WhisperX segment carries text, start and end as well, so a segment-level file parsed as a corpus of paragraph-length words with no gaps between them and reported nothing wrong. A fallback is only safe when the fallback field cannot appear on the wrong kind of object.

Match the text, not your name for it. A test written alongside a new message can assert on what the author called the thing rather than on what the function emits. expect_false(any(grepl("outlier", ...))) was written against a conditional note and satisfied by an unconditional header one line above it that happened to use the same word. The gate below compares tests/ against R/ and does not catch this, because the pattern does appear in the source. Grep the function for the pattern before asserting its absence.

Substitute the runtime values before wrapping. A message built with paste0() around a count or a name is a different length at run time than in the source, and the wrap moves with it. Harvesting the literals alone reported a test of the row-dropping message at validate.R:653 as broken by the wrap, where inserting the 6 of 6 the fixture produced puts the phrase back on one line. That assertion was rewritten out with the rest of validate_sample() and the rule it produced stands. The failure runs toward false alarms rather than toward missed staleness, which is the safer direction and still costs a patch.

Helper ordering. testthat evaluates a test file top to bottom and runs each test_that() as it reaches it. A helper defined below a test does not exist when that test runs. Check every helper against its first use.

Fixture names and shapes. Grep every fixture$field reference in new test blocks against what the fixture actually returns. And run the fixture through the shipped function, printing what the assertion will see, before writing the assertion. Three failures this session came from reasoning about a fixture rather than reading it.

Exact-set assertions. Sweep for expect_named() and expect_equal(names(...), ...) whenever a return shape changes. Check the object’s top-level names as well as its columns; those are different nouns and checking one is not checking the other.

7.3 Other standing rules

These bind. Anything phrased as what went wrong in a particular patch is in dev/decision-log.md instead, which is a record and not a rulebook.

Anchors are grepped and asserted, never recalled. A Python assert s.count(old) == 1 before each replacement. This caught complaint. being typed as complete. on the first patch of the session.

Verify claims where checkable. A Python transcription of Krippendorff’s alpha, validated against the published 0.7434 nominal and 0.8154 ordinal, is what verified all 50 constants in test-validate.R. Rebuild it rather than trusting what the R returns, so a wrong implementation fails rather than agreeing with itself.

Commit the delivered patch to the scratch tree the moment it is generated. Twice now a patch has gone out carrying the previous one’s hunks, because the scratch tree was edited for patch N+1 while its HEAD still sat at N-1. The reference is only committed when Gorsky confirms, which is right, and the next patch gets written before that confirmation arrives, which is the collision.

The rule is that generating a patch commits it as delivered, and a reported failure resets rather than the confirmation advancing. Then every diff is against the last thing that left, and a double-counted patch is unrepresentable rather than caught.

Both times the verification step passed, because it applied the patch to a tree reverted to the wrong base and got a clean result. A verification that shares the mistake with the thing it verifies is not a verification. So the base tree’s digest is checked against the one Gorsky reports before the patch is generated, not after it fails.

Simulate before asserting. Every numeric claim in a new test should be run through the shipped function first and printed. This caught a test asserting a paired bootstrap is tighter than an independent one, which is false whenever the correlation is negative.

A patch that withdraws a claim has to re-read the tests asserting it. 0008 put $coder_bins on $bins’s axis and a test pinned it. 0009 took the axis apart on the evidence of a real run, rewrote the roxygen and this document, and left the test asserting the withdrawn claim, along with its name. The suite said so on the first test().

That is 7.4’s shape a third time, and the two before it were a message reworded and a fixture changed. This one is a decision reversed, which is worse, because the test that fails is the one that was right yesterday and reading the failure tells you nothing about which of the two is now correct. So the sweep after reversing a decision is over the tests that assert it, by name and by content, before the patch goes out rather than after it fails.

The same patch also carried a test whose arithmetic was reasoned rather than run. The peer forecast is leave-one-out, so two coders leave one other and the Laplace denominator is 1 + k rather than 2 + k. 7.3 already says to simulate before asserting and the container cannot run R, which makes deriving a constant by hand the thing to distrust most, not least.

do.call() evaluates its argument list, so a language object goes in and comes out run. finish_reference() had two attributes to stamp conditionally and routed both through do.call(stamp_provenance, ...) to keep one call site. call in that list is match.call()’s language object, do.call() evaluated it, and coder_reference(ana = s$ana, ...) therefore ran inside stamp_provenance()’s frame. Four coder_reference() tests died on object 's' not found, one cause behind all of them. The direct call it replaced had never evaluated anything, because an argument that is only assigned is never forced.

quote = TRUE fixes it and the assignments were written out instead, since two attr<- lines say what they do where a quoted do.call() says it in a footnote. The rule is that do.call() takes a list of values. Anything holding a call, a formula or a symbol wants quote = TRUE or wants unrolling. The three other sites in the package pass frames and settings, which was checked rather than assumed.

This is 7.4’s shape arriving through an argument rather than through a file. Nothing about it needed a corpus or a server to find, and it cost a round trip because the container cannot run R and ?do.call was read from memory rather than opened.

A citation is not verified until the journal name is read off a source.

Do not predict runtime test counts. Assert FAIL 0 and the direction.

Sweep all of tests/, never head, never scope to the file being edited. A sweep also has to read whole calls rather than lines. Almost every call in the tests and the vignettes spans several, so a regex anchored on the opening parenthesis finds nothing, and a hit list that looks like false positives is evidence the pattern is wrong rather than that the tree is clean. Balance the parentheses and read the call. Changing a message and grepping only the file the message lives in reports the file clean and leaves an assertion in tests/ reading a string that no longer exists. This happened after the rule above was already written, so the check is now mechanical. Every expect_error, expect_message and expect_warning literal in every test file, matched against the strings R/ emits with the paste0 fragments joined first. Base R’s own messages are the only expected misses, and they are named rather than skipped.

A line citation is written file.R:NNN and re-resolved when the file is patched. The form is the path relative to the package root and the line, and a function name goes before it rather than inside it, as labels_from_instrument() at validate.R:1861 does. read_timings():220 was neither, since 220 named no file and was not a line in the one it meant. Every citation into a file a patch touches is re-resolved in that patch, because a citation nobody re-resolves decays into a number that points at whatever moved into its place.

Two Sys.time() calls are not one value. test-pipeline.R asserted that read_checkpoints() restores run_at by comparing it to the stamp on the object measure() returned. Those are different moments. ckpt_write() stamps each document as it finishes and new_results() stamps the return value after the loop, so the restored value is the earlier of the two and they print equal only while both land in the same second. It passed for months and failed once at a second boundary. A test of restored provenance asserts against what is on disk, and the same goes for anything else read back from a clock.

Confirm the base digest before building against a file the author has been reading. 0012 was built on the tree 0011 produced, while Gorsky had since made two prose edits to complete_run.qmd. git apply refused, correctly, and the patch had to be rebuilt. 0004b was the same failure with a different cause, devtools::build_vignettes() writing to .Rbuildignore. The rule that covers both is to ask for the digest of any file the last turn put in front of them, rather than assuming the tree is where the last patch left it. A rebase costs one turn; a refused patch costs two and reads as a mistake in the work.

A sealed function documents its ... or check() warns. Ten of the eleven had no @param ..., and checking Rd \usage sections reports every one, because a \usage entry must document every argument it shows. Only measure() passed, having had a ... and a @param for it already. The text says what the dots are for, which is nothing, and why they refuse rather than absorb.

Deleting a column means finding what read it, and scored_report() did. audit.R:854 carried entropy forward with .data$entropy[1] to print the header line, which 0020 broke. It is a function of prob_renorm and nothing else, so it is recomputed in the summarise that already has the group, with shannon() carrying the same formula score.R used. Flagged before 0020 was written and then not done, which is the failure worth recording rather than the fix.

A fixed join list cannot cover an argument that names columns. as_wide(keep = ) carries columns the caller asked measure() to keep, which are per document and therefore in $calls, and the preamble joined a hardcoded three. The keep names have to be passed to the join. It is the only consumer with that shape, checked rather than assumed.

Reading only $probs columns is not the same as needing no join. threshold_sensitivity() reads item, label and ok, all in $probs, so it was left without a preamble. It reads them with results[results$ok & ..., , drop = FALSE], and two-dimensional indexing on a list is an error. It flattens on the keys alone, which adds no columns and makes it a frame.

A grain change breaks index arithmetic silently, not loudly. The test-audit.R fixture sets margin on the results and then indexes it by match(s$id, res$id). Rewriting res$margin to res$calls$margin left twenty values indexed by a forty-row lookup, which recycles or returns NA rather than erroring. Three of the four sites in that file needed the index changed as well as the column, and the mechanical rewrite only did the column.

Reading indentation off a sed display is how three anchors were wrong. Every earlier look at these lines went through sed 's/^/ /', so the prefix was four spaces of my own and the anchors carried it. All three failed their assertion, which is the good outcome, but the fix was to stop matching on text and edit by line number, where indentation cannot be guessed at all.

Classifying a pipeline from its first two lines is how gold_join was missed. It opens filter(ok, label == "positive"), which is $probs throughout, and reads tone four lines further down, which is a keep column and therefore in $calls. Same for the gate’s relevant. The check that catches it follows the pipeline to its close and looks for any keep name in the whole block, rather than reading the head and inferring the rest.

Fixing a script site by site is how entropy survived three patches. The deletion sweep at 0021 printed bake_results.R:1364 reading entropy in a select(), and only R/ was fixed. It then failed on the third re-bake, after two other errors had been fixed one at a time in front of it. The audit that should have run once covers every deleted column and every results-as-frame use across data-raw/, dev/ and all four articles, and finding them together is what makes them one patch rather than four.

Making the code work is not the same as making the article say what the code does. After 0028 every chunk ran, and complete_run.qmd still opened ### What comes back with One row per document, item, and label, then used res$probs without ever telling a reader the object has two frames. The section now names both and says why the second exists, the keep column is accounted for where it shows up in names(), and the six-level table says what slice_max and the join are doing before running five verbs that used to be one filter.

A checker that classifies a line and moves on will miss a line that does two things. The article audit matched res <- baked$res_six as an assignment and skipped the rest of that line, which was %>% dplyr::select(-coded, -weight3). It reported zero issues and check() failed on the chunk. Removing the early continue so an assignment line is still examined for a use is the whole fix, and it finds nothing else across the four articles.

Rewrapping a comment needs the paragraph, and a paragraph ends at a roxygen tag. The longer name pushed ten lines past 80. Splitting each one left orphan fragments, and rewrapping the enclosing comment block merged @section and @param into the prose and swallowed a line of code that followed a comment. The working version bounds a paragraph at a tag, at a bare marker, and at the first non-comment line, and it is checked by counting ^#' @ before and after.

A column rename does reach the checkpoints, where the split did not. The split happens in new_results(), above the payload, so ckpt_write() and ckpt_read() never saw it. ckpt_stale() reads columns off the stored frame directly, so renaming ok made r$call_ok NULL on every existing payload, NULL & r$model == model logical(0), and every item stale. Seven cache directories would have re-extracted against the model, silently and at the cost of a full run. ckpt_read() now renames on read, so the two generations coexist in one directory, and a test writes an old-schema payload and asserts nothing comes back stale.

[fn()] in roxygen is a link, and a @noRd function has no topic to link to. label_levels()’s description opened with [item_levels()], which document() refuses because the target is internal and generates no .Rd. Backticks are the form for naming an internal, and the line below it already used them for score_labels(). Checked across all 99 @noRd functions in the package: no other bracket link to one exists.

Documenting the phantom cost the schema its exactness. test-regressions.R compared the documented set against setdiff(reserved_cols(), DROP_COLS) with text carved out, because the two could not otherwise agree. With the column gone the assertion is a plain equality, which is a stronger check and the one that would have caught this. test-pipeline.R’s ceiling on names($calls) becomes an equality for the same reason.

Deleting a section means checking what justified the code above it. keep = "reconciliation" existed because the confusion table joined it. The article’s Step 3 turned out not to claim that, so the argument still demonstrates what it demonstrates and SIX is still defined in the fill chunk that survives. Worth checking rather than assuming, since an earlier version of that sentence did say the column reached Step 5.

Sweep for a retired term case-insensitively. Vocabulary opening a sentence is capitalized, and a case-sensitive grep then reports the file clean. Kappa at the head of a paragraph in example_nyt.qmd and Accuracy at the head of a comment in the bake were both missed this way, one after the other.

Replace a function together with its roxygen block. The unit is the block plus the function.

A roxygen link may point outward from an @noRd block but never inward to one. [prepare_audio()] inside an internal resolves because the target is exported. [cache_settings()] does not, because a block carrying only @noRd generates no topic, and document() warns while check() stays silent since no .Rd was written to hold a cross-reference. Backticks instead. The check is one sweep of every [name()] in R/ against the set of functions whose roxygen carries @noRd, and it has caught four, two in each of two patches.

One thing that sweep cannot see. The first document() after adding a new export warns about links to it, because roxygen resolves against installed topics and the installed package predates the function. It goes away on the second pass and is not a defect.

A patch is built against the tree the previous one produced and confirmed applied. Stating the base is not enough if the base is a patch that was delivered and skipped. 0018 was built on 0017, 0017 was never run, and the apply failed on a row of the digest table this document then carried, three sections away from anything either patch was about. The diagnosis is to diff the file the person has against the base that was assumed.

One patch per message when a script goes out with it. 0017 was skipped because it shared a message with a rewritten dev/ script, and the script was what got run. Two files in one message is two things to act on and only one of them looks like an instruction.

A standing rule is one that survives its own incident. Instances go to dev/decision-log.md, and this section keeps only what tells a future editor what to do.

Markup another tool transforms is checked by rendering it. A clean gate over the source says nothing about HTML that pkgdown generates, and the rule is to say so when shipping rather than to report the gate as if it settled the question.

A prose pass over reference material ends by reading every claim against the @return it describes. A prose audit is not a claims audit, and the second is the one that matters.

A message says what happened and what to do, and a help page says why. An error that names no remedy is not shorter, it is unactionable.

A help page says what a number is. A sentence about meaning stays on the page only when it stops a wrong conclusion drawn from a correctly described number. The faq vignette that carried the rest was removed, see 5.33.

roxygen is written in markdown. DESCRIPTION carries Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE), so tables go in as GFM and component lists as ## subsections rather than \tabular and \describe, which give no containment.

index.md keeps at most three plain bullets per function. No function names inside a bullet and no term a reader would have to look up, since the reference pages carry the vocabulary and the landing page carries what each function is for. Its seven steps are closed <details> blocks, so no markdown heading may sit inside one, a blank line follows <summary> and precedes </details>, and the summary text uses <strong> rather than asterisks.

An article’s prose names the columns the chunk beneath it prints. The one eval = FALSE output block in complete_run.qmd is static text a message change does not reach, and it is found by scanning every fence for #> outside a live chunk.

A test added for a defect is run against the tree before the patch. The patch says what it showed, and a test that passes there is described as pinning a contract rather than catching a defect.

New test code is formatted by Air on its own before it goes into a file, so a file already carrying formatting drift gains none from the patch.

7.4 The recurring failure, named plainly

Six of this session’s failures share one shape. Something was changed and the things depending on it were not re-read. A message reworded and its assertion left behind, twice. A fixture made inconsistent and the tests reading it not re-run. A test’s quantity swapped while its parameters stayed. A capability added and the prose asserting its absence left standing, three times.

The gates in 7.2 cover the mechanical half. The other half is a habit. After changing anything, list what reads it, and go read those.

A second shape, and it cost more turns than the first. Something was asserted about a file that was never re-read. Three times, and each time the file in context said otherwise.

A line was handed over calling validate_sample(sheet, baked$res_gold), where sheet is defined in example_nyt.qmd and not in the bake at all. The ati codebook was asked for twice, when example_ati.qmd states it was never published. And the parlasent forced-choice run was declared absent from the payload, prompting a proposal to restructure the bake and re-run it, after searching the file for res_choice. The object is called res_sent, it is saved three lines above saveRDS, and it was the last entry in a key list printed two turns earlier.

The rule is one line. Before saying a thing is missing, absent, unsaved or unavailable, open the file and look. A search that comes back empty is evidence about the search term, not about the tree. This applies hardest right after a real instance of the same defect has been found, because auc_prob is genuinely computed after the save and that finding was generalized without checking.

A third shape, and it is the one this rule was written to stop. Something was written into the package from a description rather than from the thing described. Three more instances, all in the audio work, all caught by output Gorsky produced rather than by review.

--compute_type int8 was documented as required on macOS because the float16 default was said to raise there. It came from a web search. The help says default resolves to float32 on CPU, and a run with the flag unset reported exactly that and completed. The claim was written two patches after this rule was.

The diarizer was named pyannote 3.1 at 11 to 19 percent. WhisperX loads speaker-diarization-community-1, which the help and the run log both say, and the figure traces to an SEO comparison page rather than to pyannote, whose own table gives a range four times wider. Wrong model and wrong number, in a sentence that had been in the document for two sessions.

And read_timings() subsetted by name without checking it had a named list, so a shape with no word objects raised a subscript error instead of reaching the refusal written to describe it. Only a real file from a third recognizer could find that, because the guard is correct against every shape anyone had imagined.

The generalization is that reading a format’s documentation and reading its output are different activities, and only the second one is evidence. Every claim in 9.4 about a flag now traces to a --help that was run.

7.5 Container constraints

CRAN is blocked. R is not on PATH by default and has to be installed first. It comes from the Ubuntu archive at 4.3.3, below the R (>= 4.4.0) in DESCRIPTION, so %||% is not in base. The same archive’s r-cran-* packages cover every Import and the test Suggests, and with %||% defined in the global environment, which the base namespace falls through to, pkgload::load_all() and the whole test suite run.

A full R CMD check --as-cran runs too. micromamba installs from its GitHub release, and micromamba create -c conda-forge gives R 4.5 with every Import and Suggest, and ffmpeg in a second environment. Quarto comes from its GitHub release, since the conda build is missing a file its launcher needs. The container defaults to the C locale, so build under LANG=C.UTF-8 unless the C locale is the point. data/ and the baked results are absent, so a check here runs on stand-ins with the same columns and a stubbed model, which tests the code and not the figures.

Air 0.11.0 installs from the GitHub release (air-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz) and is what keeps the tree formatted. Prefer shortening a string over accepting Air’s rewrap when it splits a single argument onto its own line.

data/ is not available, so nothing runs against the real corpora. Gorsky runs those and pastes output.

8. Open items

None of these is a defect. They are unwritten work, coverage waiting on a corpus, and questions waiting on a decision. Anything that was a defect has been closed. Where an entry describes a limitation rather than something to repair, it says so, and 5 carries the reasoning.

8.1 Vignettes, which are the critical path

example_parlasent.qmd is closed rather than owed. Its content is the second half of complete_run.qmd, so writing it would restate a vignette that already exists. The commented entry has been removed from _pkgdown.yml rather than left as a promise.

example_validation.qmd is not planned. Its subject was the sampling design on the nyt relevance corpus, and both are gone, the design with 5.30 and the corpus with 5.32. Its commented entry has been removed from _pkgdown.yml.

An images vignette joins it and needs a corpus with publishable rights.

faq was removed until real questions arrive, see 5.33. It held what the help pages used to say about reading their output. interpreting-validation held what the validation help pages used to say about their figures, including the decision table, and was dropped for now.

8.2 Still open

interpreting-validation.Rmd was dropped for now. Its text was not moved into any other document, by decision, and what becomes of it is still to be settled.

The FAQ comes back when real questions arrive. The removed faq.Rmd is in git history, and its answers on which endorsement rate to report, the saturation pair and the diagnostics are the ones the help pages used to point to.

The NYT example could return on individual crowd ratings. The replication README describes ground-truth-dataset-cf.csv as the labels ten coders gave the set used as ground truth, which is CF Truth, and a06-reliability.R produces the appendix table on reliability, which should say which file carries coder-level rows and what agreement the authors found among their own coders. If the ratings are coder-level, laying them out as rating slots, the first rating on each article in one sheet and the second in another, gives validate_sample() a list whose gap sets the local LLM against two random crowd workers. Binarizing nine-point ratings, the 5s included, is a decision that comes first. nyt and nyt_gold were removed as well, so a return starts by building a dataset from that file.

What is left is narrower and still true. b_six carries no scores, since its labels are numerals and a score vector over them is an identity map, so the scale reaches those calls through labels instead. b_tone is the only instrument in the payload that does carry scores, and res_tone’s human column is tone_mean, a continuous average rather than a label, so there is nothing to put in human_label without inventing a cut. expected_score against a human figure is therefore fixtures only until an article supplies one.

A forced aligner can stretch a segment-final word across trailing silence, putting a pause inside a word instead of after it. It belongs to the timing half, which ships, and 9.4 records the case.

The timing experiment 9.2 committed to has not been run. Run an instrument with annotate_timing on and again with it off on one corpus, and read the two against each other with the gap validate_sample() reports. If the markers do not move the answers they are token cost, and that is a finding about whether the construct lives in delivery.

The intended audio test corpus cannot ship. It is a six-minute film scene with two speakers and a wide tonal range. It is copyrighted, so it is usable for developing the method and cannot ship in a vignette. It also has no paired design, since each line is spoken once, so the test is not calm against angry on the same words. It is a natural corpus with no labels, which makes the check coding_sample() on the utterances and validate_sample() against a hand coding, on sixty to a hundred units rather than five pairs.

Constants whose reasons are not recorded. Each wants a one-line reason in the code or a decision recorded in 5. The ones already answered are left off this list, keep_alive by 5.17.

  • resolve_num_ctx() refuses an explicit ceiling below 512, and under "auto" floors at 2048, adds 1.25 times the measured prompt, and flags a count no more than 8 above a multiple of 1024.
  • measure() flags truncation within 64 tokens of num_ctx, warns about checkpointing above 2000 calls, and prints progress every tenth document.
  • Checkpoint file stems are capped at 96 characters with an 8-character md5 suffix, and the prompt hash keeps 12 characters.
  • timeout defaults to 600 seconds, TAGS_TIMEOUT is 15, ollama_modalities() waits 5, and the model listing sizes its name column to 32 characters.
  • item_report() counts pct_extreme_renorm at 0.01 and 0.99.
  • coding_sample() defaults to n = 200, inspect_cases() shows 6 cases, and threshold_sensitivity() sweeps 0.1 to 0.9.
  • prepare_video() cuts frames at JPEG quality 3 and audio at 16 kHz mono, and run_recognizer() keeps the last 25 lines of a failed run.
  • read_checkpoints() takes the instrument, the backend and num_ctx from the first readable payload in directory-listing order.

Figures quoted in code without their runs in the repository. instrument() cites a sweep of ten Ollama models across six tokenizer families, probe_labels() cites gemma4 emitting BU for BUDGET, and test-backend.R cites a thirteen-model sweep of chat templates. Each wants a pointer to 6 or to a dev/ script, which is what 5.8 asks of a figure.

5 is still append-only in places. Where an entry supersedes an earlier one, the earlier one should be rewritten rather than left at the same weight.

8.3 Settled, and recorded so it is not reopened

Both of these are in or around the validation section and both are closed. The heading said three and only two were ever written down, so if a third existed it is not recoverable from this document and will have to surface on its own.

The six-to-three collapse is stated twice and verified twice. fold3() in the bake and collapse3() in complete_run.qmd are the same rule. Both are needed, since the annotator columns ship only on six levels and both files score them on three, and neither file can reach the other. Deduplicating would mean a new export for one dataset’s coding scheme.

What was wrong was that only one of them checked itself. Both now run the rule on reconciliation and compare against parlasent$label, which is that collapse and so is the authority. Any change to either that breaks the correspondence fails immediately, in the render or in the bake. The duplication stands and the drift risk does not.

9. Multimodal, built

Shipped. prepare_image(), prepare_audio() and prepare_video() are exported, the stems have four media sets, and check_backend() probes images. What follows is the record of building it rather than a proposal, and the sections read in the order the work happened, so a later one corrects an earlier one wherever the two disagree. Nothing here is on the critical path and none of it changes anything downstream of measure(). What is left is named at the end of 9.5, and it is the native audio path and an images vignette.

9.1 What the probe settled, and what it cost to settle

dev/probe_multimodal.R sends fathom’s own request shape, copied from ollama_generate(), and reads resp$logprobs[[1]]$top_logprobs, which is the path measure.R:89 reads. So its results are results about measure().

Images keep the distribution. Against gemma4:31b at Ollama 0.32.15, a solid red PNG with a one-word question returned 20 logprobs, top1 YES at 1.000, correct. measure(image =) is buildable today, and PDF pages and video frames reduce to images.

/api/generate does not take audio. Fields named audio and audios both returned HTTP 200 with Please at 0.994, which is a model answering a question about audio it never received. A control sending a field named zzzz returned the same token at the same probability, and so did sending no field at all.

That was later found to be true of the endpoint rather than of Ollama. 9.7 has the measurement. The compatibility endpoint takes audio, and this section generalised one URL into a claim about a server. The probe was right and the sentence it produced was wider than the evidence.

The control is the finding, not the audio answer. The server discards unknown top-level fields without complaint. So fathom cannot send a modality and wait to be told no. It gets a fluent answer built from nothing, and a corpus run completes looking healthy. That is the Images are accepted and ignored failure one modality over, and it is why 9.2 has both a declared capability and a probe.

The first version of that script reported the audio field as a PASS, because verdict() asked only whether logprobs came back. A run that completes looking healthy while testing nothing, which is worse than a failure.

Its timing block was confounded the same way and had to be rebuilt. It compared one image with K questions against K images with one question, so one arm sent a byte-identical prompt on every call and the other did not, and prompt prefix caching alone accounts for the 2.47 ratio it produced. It also built the images inside the timed block. The replacement runs three arms varying one thing each, same image and same question as the floor, then a new question, then a new image, with everything encoded before the clock starts.

What the confounded run did settle is correctness. Six questions about a red square came back YES NO NO NO NO YES, which is six right answers, so the Qwen3-VL and Gemma3 report of a cache answering instead of the model is not firing on gemma4.

A vision model reads a spectrogram and will not answer an affect question about one. Asked whether a spectrogram showed a loud energetic utterance, gemma4 gave 0.276 on a shouted clip against 0.105 on a calm one, which is a live answer tracking the truth. Asked whether the speaker sounded angry, it answered NO at better than 0.999 to every representation including a paragraph of prosody numbers, which has nothing to do with pictures. The model is not failing to discriminate. It is refusing a question it reads as literally unanswerable, since it received an image and nothing sounds like anything.

Three things had to be fixed before that reading was fair, and each was a defect in the probe rather than in the model. Log magnitude stretched between the observed minimum and maximum let one near-silent bin pin the floor at -100 dB and crush all real speech into the top sixth of the range, so the quieter clip came out a featureless grey and the model was choosing between a spectrogram and a blank. The waveform plotted every sample into 448 pixels and was solid ink. And three decimal places reported a pair as ordered when both values were 0.000 and the difference was rounding.

The literature agrees and does not transfer. Spectrograms into vision models for speech emotion is mature, and every result in it trains. Dixit, Heller and Donahue get GPT-4o to 59% on ESC-10 and beat human experts on visual spectrogram classification, and the word in their title is few-shot. They prompt with labeled example spectrograms of each class. That is not the regime this package works in, and adopting it would cost the zero-shot claim in 1.

9.2 The design

Three input columns. measure(x, backend, instrument, text =, image =, audio =), later video =, naming file paths except text. Any combination on a row. There is no mode = argument, because which columns were built is the branch, so nothing needs renaming when a backend gains a modality.

Backends declare what they take. ollama_backend(modalities = c("text", "image")) as a fact about the server. measure() refuses an undeclared column locally, before the first call.

And check_backend() proves the declaration rather than trusting it. Two calls, same question, different images. Identical distributions mean the image never reached the model. That is the zzzz control generalized, it separates ignored from wrong where one call cannot, and it costs two startup calls only when images are in play. An eighth documented failure, so the guard in test-regressions.R goes from seven to eight.

Helpers return objects and never perform hidden steps. d <- prepare_audio(files) then measure(d, ...), never measure(files, transcribe = TRUE). The middle object is inspectable, cacheable and re-runnable without paying for the transcription twice, which is coding_sample() returning a sheet rather than validate_sample() reaching out and coding for you.

Each object carries its quality on it, in the shape prob_other already has. Characters extracted per page and whether a text layer existed. The fps actually used. The transcriber, its model, and the language detected. Every parameter that changes the measurement is an argument and lands in the returned object. A hidden default is the version 5.2 forbids.

Provenance travels as column and attribute, per the reasoning 5.14 once gave for drawn_n. A results table mixing transcript rows and native-audio rows with nothing distinguishing them is unreadable.

Audio arrives as an annotated transcript. A plain transcript discards prosody, emphasis, pace, hesitation and overlap, and for a construct that lives in delivery that is the absence of the thing being measured. Native audio would solve it and needs hardware that is not in the room. So the delivery is written into the transcript instead, which is what conversation analysis has done since the 1970s.

Jefferson notation marks pauses in tenths of a second, overlaps, emphasis, stretched sounds and sharp rises in pitch. A political scientist reads one as data. So does a model, and measure(text = ) takes it today.

I already (0.4) told you (1.1) about ↑THIS ye:sterday.

Timing is measured, not theorized, and that is what makes this different from picking acoustic features. Choosing pitch variance and asking about anger asserts that anger is pitch variance, and the interpreting has happened before the model sees anything. A 3.2 second pause is a fact. Speech rate is counted. The model does the reading.

Nothing acoustic extends it, and both attempts to are recorded in 9.4. Earlier drafts of this section promised [118 Hz, 62 dB] per word on the argument that a contour is closer to the signal than a summary statistic is to a theory. The argument still holds. What failed is the premise underneath it, that a per-word figure is available.

Pitch was not measurable to within an octave on a seventh of words. Loudness was measured exactly and could not be attached to a word, since the same speaker’s of came back at +7dB and -11dB in one clip.

So what the recording contributes is what the recognizer measures directly, which is who spoke and when they stopped. Both are exact and neither is a representation choice beyond how they are written down. What makes the choice answerable rather than assumed is that the package can measure its cost. Transcript alone against transcript plus contour on the same corpus, read with the gap validate_sample() reports, which is the two-mechanism comparison already in complete_run.qmd.

Nothing about this needs a server, a key, or CUDA. The tools sit outside fathom and hand it a text column.

Ollama takes a vector of images, and that finding removed a whole section of this plan. One picture cost 86 prompt tokens, two cost 137, four cost 239. Fifty-one tokens each, linear, so every one is encoded rather than the first being kept and the rest dropped. And the answers depend on all of them, since two red squares came back YES to whether they were the same color and a red and a blue came back NO.

The token count is the half that matters, because it is mechanical and cannot be confounded by the model being good or bad at a task. Video as frames is therefore reachable on the hardware in the room, and 9.4 no longer needs a second server to get there.

An image corpus shares no prompt prefix across items. build_prompt() puts the document first so K questions about one document differ only at the end, which is why complete_run.qmd says the text goes first and why Ollama’s longest-common-prefix cache prefills a document once rather than once per call. With an image and no text, the question is the first thing in the prompt, so K items produce K prompts that differ from token one. Whether the image embeddings are prepended into the token stream and recover the shared prefix is what the rebuilt probe’s B arm measures, and the answer decides what num_ctx = "auto" should do rather than being a curiosity.

A corpus with no text gets no document block. Text: "" asserts a document that is empty rather than one that is elsewhere, and spends the tokens to do it on every call. No placeholder replaces it. A marker tells the model nothing its own embeddings do not carry, and a file name would be worse, since angry_protest_042.png in the prompt is the name answering the question instead of the picture and nothing in the results would show it.

preview() prints a bracketed line where the document would sit, shown and never sent. Square brackets mark the function describing what travels beside the prompt rather than quoting what is inside it, which is what the scoring block below it already does. The same shape carries to audio and video.

[image: 22,873 bytes, sent alongside the prompt]

And the prompt shape is in prompt_hash(). Omitting the block changes the prompt without changing anything else in the key, so the same instrument against the same model produced two prompts and one fingerprint. A text run’s checkpoints would have read as current for an image run and been resumed into. has_text defaults to TRUE, so nothing already written moves.

What is untouched. Everything downstream of measure(). Probabilities and human labels do not change shape.

measure(image =) is in. The path threads measure.data.frame to measure_doc to measure_one to ollama_generate, which gains an images array only when there is one, so a text run sends the body it always sent. text gains a default and the guard becomes at least one of text or image.

ollama_backend(modalities = c("text", "image")) declares what the server takes and measure() refuses an undeclared column locally, before any call. Then check_backend() proves the declaration with two pictures and one question, because a declaration is not evidence when the server answers 200 to a field it does not recognize. Its @return goes from seven failures to nine, the second new one being the image probe failing rather than the image being ignored, since the remedies differ.

num_ctx = "auto" measures rather than refusing, which reverses what this section said twice. resolve_num_ctx() never estimated. It sends the longest document with the wordiest item and reads prompt_eval_count off the reply, and that count includes the image tokens because PostTokenize interleaves the embeddings before the prompt is evaluated. So the only change is which document it probes with, file size instead of word count, and the proxy has to rank rather than predict. The single-document early return is exempted for images, where the probe returns a real count for the one picture there is.

What the timings cost. Against gemma4 at 224 by 224, a fully cached call is 0.12s, a new question is 4.2x that and a new image 5.0x. So nothing is shared across a run and a corpus costs documents times items at close to full price. The marginal cost of a new image over a new question is 0.10s, so the encode is not what dominates. Correctness is clean, six questions about a red square answered right and six colors judged right on one question.

Done so far. prepare_image() turns a vector of paths into a corpus with id, image, bytes, exists and ext, decoding nothing. coding_sample(image =, copy_media = TRUE) copies the referenced files into <sheet>_media/ beside the CSV and rewrites the column relative to it, which is 5.14’s property applied to media rather than to a drawn count.

hash.R needs nothing, contrary to what this section said. prompt_hash() covers question, cue, labels and model and excludes the document by design, and checkpoint.R:22 hashes the id rather than the content. So an image changes neither.

What generalizes. Done. texts is docs in the audit functions, and hash.R hashing bytes remains. corpus_bias(), which binned on any numeric column such as bytes, was later cut. See 5.31.

What needs work. coding_sample() gains a file column, and coding_sample(file =) copies referenced media into a folder beside the CSV so the sheet stays self-contained, which is what 5.14 protected. inspect_cases() gains a format emitting a renderable path.

What refuses. num_ctx = "auto" measures when a row carries media rather than estimating, since image token cost is model-specific tiling and 5.2 forbids the guess. The revision below has how.

9.3 Everything stays in-house, and that was a decision

openai_compatible() was designed, scoped and then dropped. Its whole argument was being the socket a native audio and video server plugs into. Video as frames turned out to be reachable through Ollama, derived audio always was, and native audio was believed to need a CUDA or ROCm machine, so the socket had nothing left to plug in that could not already be reached.

The last of those turned out to be false and the conclusion still holds. 9.7 records native audio working on Apple Silicon through Ollama’s own compatibility endpoint, so no second server is needed for it either. openai_compatible() would have been the wrong shape regardless, since what the native path wants is a different endpoint on the same host rather than a different host.

What it would have bought is not worth its weight. Hosted models nobody can run locally, which are not reproducible in a paper, since gpt-4o-2024-08-06 gets retired and a pinned local tag does not. And the secondary benefit of an API key, against a package whose strongest sentence is that everything runs locally so it is usable on data that cannot be sent anywhere else.

That is the sharp difference from quallmer, which calls a hosted model by default and reaches Whisper through an API. This package runs on the machine in the room, and dropping the hosted path is what makes that true rather than nearly true.

The verified provider facts are kept because they cost work to establish and would otherwise be re-derived. OpenAI exposes top_logprobs from 0 to 20. Together documents it. vLLM serves it and adds prompt_logprobs. Groq lists logprobs and top_logprobs as unsupported and returns HTTP 400. Gemini supports response_logprobs on its native endpoint and not under OpenAI compatibility. Of four named from memory in one message, one was wrong and one was unchecked, which is why a check beats a table.

Native audio and video are unreachable here, and the backend says so. ollama_backend() refuses either word in modalities until a native path sends one, and points at prepare_audio() and prepare_video() instead. vLLM serves Qwen3-Omni with -tp 1, one GPU, and Qwen’s own model card gives the command. vllm-metal is vision-only and its two multimodal entries say image input, no video, so an Apple Silicon machine cannot be that server. The day one is available, the work is the content array serialization and a base_url, and this section is where to start reading.

9.4 What was built, and the decisions it took

Two probe scripts live in dev/ and their results are written up above, so neither needs rerunning. probe_multimodal.R settled that Ollama discards unknown fields silently, that images reach the model, and that the images array takes a vector. probe_audio_affect.R settled that a vision model reads a spectrogram and refuses an affect question about one.

unit, pause and window are gone, and the reasoning is worth keeping. Rows were the only thing unit decided, and once one recording is one row there is nothing left for it to decide. A conversation read a line at a time is not the conversation, and no question worth asking is put to a single line of dialogue. That took pause with it. A within-turn line break says only that a silence passed a threshold, where [pause 0.4s] says how long it was, so the break was a worse encoding of a fact the annotation already carried better. Cowan and NaturalTurn leave the references with it, since there is no longer a threshold to justify. Stivers stays, repurposed, and now explains why the function will not infer turns from silence when diarization is absent.

window had no literature behind it. Turn constructional units and inter-pausal units are found in the talk. A fixed bin is imposed, and it comes from continuous affect annotation and frame-based audio analysis rather than from any account of how talk divides. In a design arguing that timing is measured rather than theorized, it was the one unit that was neither. It also split mid-turn on diarized audio, putting two speakers in one row with speaker coming back NA and nothing in the text saying so, which is the silently-wrong-corpus class read_timings() already refuses at prepare.R:1126.

A silence is written as [pause] or [gap] by whether the timings carry a speaker, not by whether labels were asked for. Whether a silence is hesitation or turn transition is a fact about the recording. Tying the distinction to the rendering instead put three markers in the text against a count of two on the same row, which is how it was caught.

Every count describes the recording and only text and annotate_timing describe the rendering. n_pauses holds with annotate_timing off, where the text shows nothing.

Four more of them, all free and none reaching the model. speech_rate over the whole recording and articulation_rate over voiced time only, because someone can be fast on the clock through talking quickly or through never stopping, and the ratio between the two is the pausing. On one clip the reporter was 37 percent faster than the other speaker on the clock and 10 percent faster while actually speaking. median_turn_s, which needs turns. And median_score, the aligner’s own confidence, which read_timings() was parsing and throwing away. Thirteen of sixty-nine words on that clip were placed at under 0.3, and every [pause] figure rests on the boundaries those describe.

The first two are candidate confounds, the last is what makes subset(d, median_score > 0.5) possible. That is the whole argument for them. measure() reads id and text and nothing else, so a column costs no prompt token, and the case for one is that it is free at parse time and unrecoverable afterwards. Once the transcript is a string the silences are visible in it as characters and gone from it as data.

And the thing that would actually change an answer needs no new column. Run the instrument with annotate_timing on and again with it off on one corpus and read them against each other with the gap validate_sample() reports. If the markers do not move the answers they are token cost, and that is a finding about whether the construct lives in delivery. 9.2 committed to that experiment and it has never been run. It also moves with diarization on the same words, 2 against 3 on the fixture, because without turns a turn transition is just another silence. That the two differ is the diarization saying something.

Neither pitch nor loudness ships, and both were built before being removed.

Pitch was measured out first. Nine synthetic signals of known fundamental were built to provoke the three failures this section recorded, an octave-up trap with the second harmonic loudest, a missing fundamental, and sub-harmonic energy. seewave::fund() and wrassp::ksvF0() both passed all nine, and seewave::autoc() failed every one, so the earlier autocorrelation attempts were the method rather than the difficulty. fund() also returns the same 120.3 on every 120 Hz signal, which is not accuracy but the cepstral peak landing on an integer sample lag.

Then the same two estimators went at clean dialogue. They agreed within a semitone on twelve words in fourteen and disagreed by ten and by twelve point seven semitones on the other two, with nothing in the output marking which. A quarter of words yielded no voiced frame at all, including fire, a voiced diphthong of 280 milliseconds. Sweeping minAmp from 50 to 0 changed the voiced fraction not at all, and constraining the range per speaker to two thirds and one and a half times its median made it worse, from 0.45 down to 0.36 and 0.27, because a range does not resolve an octave error, it discards the frame.

So the sentence this section already carried applies to the finished attempt as much as to the abandoned ones. A biased pitch value in a measurement package produces a wrong finding quietly, so it does not exist rather than existing badly. Right six times in seven and octave-wrong the rest, with the wrong ones unmarked, is that.

Then loudness shipped, and was removed a day later. wrassp::rmsana() is exact, reproducing 6 dB steps at 6.02, 12.04 and 18.06 on a synthetic file, and it needs no range, no gender and no voicing decision. It was rendered as [+9dB], a deviation from the speaker’s median, on the argument that emphasis is the thing a transcript cannot carry.

The clip refuted it. At min_db = 3 it marked 55 percent of words, and db_iqr came back 7.7, so the default sat well inside ordinary variation. That alone was a bad default rather than a bad feature. What killed it was the ranked extremes. The same speaker’s of appeared at +6.6dB and -11.4dB, and lot at +6.7dB and -12.5dB, so two words held both ends of the same distribution in twenty-four seconds. No threshold separates that, because both extremes survive any of them. Meanwhile not, bracketed by two pauses and the one word a reader would underline, came back unmarked.

Nor was it a short-word artefact, which was the hypothesis. Words under five frames had a smaller mean deviation than the rest, 2.6 against 4.6.

The RMS is right. What is wrong is the interval it is handed, since a word boundary from a forced aligner is not a stable unit for level. Bravia. was given 315 frames for one word, 1.58 seconds, because the aligner stretched a segment-final word across the trailing silence. That is worth pursuing on its own account, since it affects the timing half, which does ship.

wrassp came in and went out again, and tuneR and seewave never entered. Nothing acoustic is in Suggests.

Both are off by default, so a bare call is a plain transcript needing no token and no diarizer. Nothing is implied by a shorthand any more.

prepare_pdf() is dropped. pdftools needs poppler, which is a system library rather than an R package, so it would put a build dependency on every machine that renders the site. Gorsky decided against it. A PDF corpus is reachable today by rasterizing outside the package and handing the pages to prepare_image(), which is the same route 9.1 established when it found that pages and frames both reduce to images.

prepare_audio() takes the audio and runs the recognizer itself. An earlier draft had it take JSON only, with the user running one command in a terminal first. Gorsky overruled that twice and was right both times. The rule it rested on, that helpers return objects and never perform hidden steps, was written to stop measure() transcribing behind the caller’s back. A named function whose entire job is preparing audio is not a hidden step, and applying the rule there was applying it past the case it was written for.

Two switches, and getting there took four goes. The first was a multi-value annotate with several.ok = TRUE. Gorsky rejected it because the other seventeen match.arg() calls in the package are single-select, and he was right. The second was single-select with "all" as a shorthand, which worked while there were two renderings. Adding loudness broke it, since one choice argument cannot express three independent things, and the repair was to invent "transcript" for the pair. Two invented values to undo a constraint that never applied.

Gorsky’s objection settled it. Speaker, timing and loudness were never alternatives, they compose, so they became three booleans. "all", "none" and "transcript" all go, expand_annotate() goes, and so do three refusals that existed only to catch combinations a shorthand could imply. The single-select rule holds for choices between alternatives, which these are not. Loudness went a day later on the evidence above, and the two that remain are booleans for the reason three were.

The prefixes carry the layer and that is load-bearing. diarize_names is a transcription setting, in the cache key beside asr_model, and switching it re-transcribes. annotate_timing is free, touches no file, and stays out of the key.

And diarize_names decides whether the text has turns at all, not only whether labels are printed. A turn is a run of words by one speaker, so without diarization there are none, every silence is a [pause] rather than a [gap], and n_turns, n_speakers and n_gaps are NA. Off, the speaker column is ignored outright rather than merely unprinted, so a hand-corrected transcript that happens to carry speakers cannot break the text into lines behind the caller’s back.

extra is the twenty flags that do not earn a name. --beam_size, --temperature, --no_speech_threshold, --vad_onset and the rest reach the recognizer and come back as something this never reads, so naming one and not the others is a choice a reader would ask about. A named argument earns its name by having work done with it here, which is why diarize decides whether hf_token is required and asr_model lands on the row. Four flags are refused in extra because the function depends on them, --output_format, --output_dir, --no_align and --diarize.

verbosity is the three levels measure() already has. These tools print tens of lines about their own dependencies on every invocation, and forty recordings would bury everything else. At "normal" the output is captured and fathom prints one line per recording instead. Captured rather than discarded, so a failing call carries the last 25 lines in the condition rather than pointing at scrollback.

One export. Transcription lives in an internal @noRd helper beside read_timings(), rename_speakers(), turns_of(), within_gaps() and render_turn(), because process handling and cache checking have no business inside the annotation logic. Nobody calls it.

Audio is the only input, and that is the third overrule. The first draft took JSON only. The signature above took either. Gorsky removed the JSON branch as well, on the grounds that a corpus reaching measure() starts from recordings and nothing else, so a second entry point serves a case that does not arise. That is also what finally makes the name true, since the function has so far read JSON and never opened an audio file.

The cache covers what the JSON argument was covering. A hand-corrected transcript is the case worth protecting, since ASR gets proper nouns wrong and a researcher fixes them. Edit the JSON beside the audio and the next call reads it rather than the recognizer.

And it keys on the settings, which took a second pass to get right. The first version keyed on the audio path alone, so diarize = FALSE in a directory already holding a diarized transcript read the diarized one and ignored the argument. asr_model, language and extra had the same hole. It surfaced when the exercise script needed three separate cache_dir values to demonstrate the function, which is a workaround standing in for a defect.

ckpt_stale() had the answer already. It calls a checkpoint current only if it succeeded under this model with this prompt hash, so settings are the key rather than identity. The same question here, with the settings in a .fathom.json beside each transcript, since the recognizer owns the transcript itself and a researcher may edit it.

Four states rather than two, because the artifact is external. "absent" for missing, older than the recording, or unreadable, that last one for ckpt_read()’s reason, that a run killed mid-write leaves one and re-transcribing is the only recoverable reading. "stale" for made under other settings. "current" for made under these. And "unverified" for usable with no record beside it, which is the hand-corrected transcript, used rather than discarded, with tool, asr_model and extra coming back NA instead of naming settings that did not produce those words.

min_pause and speakers are deliberately outside the key. Neither reaches the recognizer, so changing a rendering re-reads the same transcript rather than paying for an hour of audio again.

It costs the offline example and most of the offline tests. The roxygen example runs today from a literal word list, with no audio and no recognizer installed, which is why it is a good example. Mandatory audio makes it \dontrun{} or ties it to a fixture in inst/extdata, and neither is as good. The rendering tests move to fathom::: against word tables, which is how the package already tests, and the public function keeps a missing path and a refused combination and nothing that exercises the annotation. Accept that deliberately rather than discovering it at check().

And annotate = "none" is one row of plain text per recording, which is the simplest thing anyone wants and has to be easy to reach. quallmer produces that shape by calling openai::create_transcription() in a purrr loop inside the vignette, against the hosted whisper-1 endpoint, and reports the dollar cost. This does it locally in one call, which is the difference 9.3 is about.

whisperx is the default and the order of that vector is why. match.arg() takes the first, and whisperx runs on macOS, Linux and Windows where whispermlx is Apple Silicon only. Their help texts differ in one option out of forty, --device defaulting to cpu against mps, so whispermlx is the same tool with an MLX backend, faster on that hardware and emitting identical JSON. On one clip they produced the same 69 words, the same n_pauses, n_gaps and median_gap_s, and differed only in gonna against going to and an um... one of them dropped. Same aligner, same diarizer, so the choice moves the words and not the timings.

parakeet-mlx was dropped, and not for the reason the earlier draft gave. It was described as not diarizing and therefore suiting one speaker. Its actual output has no word field at any level. --highlight-words gives sub-word pieces, 127 tokens for 67 words, and they reassemble on a leading-space rule only to land in the wrong place. It puts Superman. at 0.24 to 1.76 where WhisperX puts it at 0.251 to 0.811, because sentence-final punctuation is emitted as its own token half a second after the word ends and reassembly hands that tail to the word. Every boundary carries it, and every time lands on an 0.08 second grid against WhisperX’s 0.001. Pauses measured off it would be fiction. A reassembly helper was considered and is not the hard part, which is why it is not the reason.

Three things it has to get right.

It cannot install the recognizer. uv tool install whisperx is one command and R has no business running a package manager. It checks Sys.which() and refuses with the exact install line for the tool that was asked for.

It has to cache. An hour of audio takes about a minute, and nobody should pay that twice for re-running a chunk. A transcript on disk made under these settings is reused, and force = TRUE overrides.

And tool is explicit with no silent fallback, since a run that quietly used a different recognizer is a corpus nobody can reproduce. SystemRequirements gains a line naming both, marked optional, since the annotation half runs without either.

Five things about the tool, read off it rather than recalled.

asr_model rather than model, since backend$model is the LLM and both reach the same results table. The default is large-v3 outright, which reverses what this section said before. The argument for resolving per tool was that the naming schemes differ, and the tool that made them differ was parakeet. With it gone, whispermlx --model large-v3 maps the short name to mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-mlx itself, so both remaining tools take the same string. It is not left unset either, since the CLI default is small and tiny on one clip turned I did into My dead.

The model that argument names is the least load-bearing of three. WhisperX runs faster-whisper, then wav2vec2 forced alignment, then a diarizer. Whisper’s native segment timestamps drift by hundreds of milliseconds, which is the order of min_pause itself, so the alignment pass produced every [pause] and [gap] this function writes. The aligner is selected automatically from the language code and the WhisperX paper found a larger one unhelpful, so it is not an argument.

The diarizer is pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1, not 3.1, read off --diarize_model in the help and confirmed in the run log. The 11 to 19 percent this section carried was wrong twice over, naming a model that does not run and quoting a figure that traces to an SEO comparison page rather than to pyannote. Their own table gives community-1 from 8.9 percent on REPERE to 46.8 on Ego4D across twelve benchmarks, scored with no forgiveness collar and without skipping overlapping speech, and gives 3.1 a wider range still. The spread is the corpus rather than the model, which is a better argument for coding_sample() on a diarized corpus than a tight-looking range was.

--no_align must never be passed. It returns segment-level output with no word timings, which read_timings() already refuses at prepare.R:1126 with the right message.

No compute type is set, and the paragraph that said otherwise was wrong. This section claimed --compute_type int8 was required on macOS because the float16 default raises there. The help says default resolves to float16 on GPU and float32 on CPU, and a run on Apple Silicon with the flag unset reported defaulting to float32 for device cpu and completed. The claim came from a web search rather than from the tool, two patches after 7.4 was written to stop exactly that.

whispermlx remains the Apple Silicon recommendation, since CTranslate2 has no Metal backend and MLX does use the GPU. That is a speed argument rather than a correctness one.

min_speakers and max_speakers are the cheapest reduction available in the diarization error rate above. An interview has two speakers and the researcher knows it before transcribing.

It is built, and the reason it took six patches is worth keeping. The flags were read off whisperx --help and whispermlx --help, and the parser was checked against four real files, three from the whisper family and one from parakeet.
